X​YXY-VBS phase boundary for the square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} X​X​ZXXZ model with the ring exchange

Yoshihiro Nishiyama Affiliation: Department of Physics, Faculty of Science, Okayama University, Okayama 700-8530, Japan
Received: date / Accepted: date
Abstract

The square-lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} X​X​ZXXZ model with the ring-exchange interaction KK was investigated numerically. As for the hard-core-boson model with the nearest-neighbor hopping J1/2J_{1}/2, namely, the J1J_{1}-KK X​YXY model, it has been reported that the ring exchange leads to a variety of exotic phases such as the valence-bond-solid (VBS) phase. In this paper, we extend the parameter space in order to investigate the phase boundary between the X​YXY (superfluid) and VBS phases. A notable feature is that the phase boundary terminates at the fully-frustrated point, J2/J1→0.5−J_{2}/J_{1}\to 0.5^{-}. As a scaling parameter for the multi-criticality, the distance from the multi-critical point δ(≥0)\delta(\geq 0) is introduced. In order to detect the phase transition, we employed the high-order fidelity susceptibility χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F}, which is readily evaluated via the exact-diagonalization scheme. As a demonstration, for a fixed value of δ\delta, the X​YXY-VBS criticality was analyzed by the probe χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F}. Thereby, with properly scaling δ\delta, the χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F} data were cast into the crossover-scaling formula to determine the multi-criticality.

1 Introduction

The two-dimensional hard-core boson model with the nearest-neighbor-hopping amplitude J1/2J_{1}/2 and the ring exchange around each plaquette KK has been investigated extensively [1, 2]. It has been shown that the ring exchange leads to a variety of exotic phases such as the valence-bond-solid (VBS) phase. The model is equivalent to the spin-S=1/2S=1/2 JJ-KK X​YXY magnet [1]. Meanwhile, the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} X​X​ZXXZ model was investigated with the coupled cluster method to surmount the negative sign problem [3]; it has to be mentioned that a limiting case, namely, the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} X​YXY model, has been studied with the tensor-network [4] and density-matrix-renormalization-group [5] methods in depth. The J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} X​X​ZXXZ model is equivalent to the hard-core-boson model with the “kinetic frustration” J2J_{2} [6], and the first- and second-neighbor Coulomb repulsions. The VBS phase is stabilized by the kinetic frustration as well as the Coulomb repulsions. A notable feature is that the phase boundary between the X​YXY (superfluid) and VBS phases terminates at the fully frustrated point J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 eventually. Such a J2J_{2}-mediated multi-criticality poses an intriguing problem.

In this paper, we investigate the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-KK X​X​ZXXZ model by means of the exact-diagonalization method. Our main concern is to investigate the X​YXY-VBS phase boundary from the viewpoint of the extended parameter space. In order to detect the X​YXY-VBS phase transition, we employ the “high order” [7, 8] fidelity susceptibility [9, 10, 11, 12, 13], which is readily evaluated via the exact diagonalization scheme. The high-order fidelity susceptibility is also applied to the analysis of the multi-criticality toward J2/J1→0.5−J_{2}/J_{1}\to 0.5^{-}.

To be specific, we present the Hamiltonian for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-KK X​X​ZXXZ model

ℋ\displaystyle{\cal H} =\displaystyle= −J1∑⟨i​j⟩(SixSjx+SiySjy)+J1Δ∑⟨i​j⟩SizSjz+J2∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩(SixSjx+SiySjy)\displaystyle-J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j})+J_{1}\Delta\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}) (1)
+J2Δ∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩SizSjz+K∑[i​j​k​l](Si+Sk+Sj−Sl−+Sl+Sj+Sk−Si−).\displaystyle+J_{2}\Delta\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}+K\sum_{[ijkl]}(S^{+}_{i}S^{+}_{k}S^{-}_{j}S^{-}_{l}+S^{+}_{l}S^{+}_{j}S^{-}_{k}S^{-}_{i}).

Here, the quantum spin-1/21/2 operators {𝐒i}\{{\bf S}_{i}\} are placed at each square-lattice point, i=1,2,…,Ni=1,2,\dots,N (NN: total number of spins), and the symbols {Si±}\{S^{\pm}_{i}\} denote the ladder operators. The summations, ∑⟨i​j⟩\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} and ∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}, run over all possible nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle and ⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle, respectively. Similarly, the summation ∑[i​j​k​l]\sum_{[ijkl]} runs over all possible plaquette spins, [i​j​k​l][ijkl]; here, the indices are arranged like □kjli{}^{i}_{l}\Box^{j}_{k} around each plaquette, □\Box. The parameters, J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and KK, denote the nearest-neighbor, next-nearest-neighbor, and ring exchange interactions, respectively, and the anisotropy parameter is given by Δ\Delta. Hereafter, the nearest-neighbor interaction J1J_{1} is regarded as the unit of energy, i.e., J1=1J_{1}=1. In the hard-core-boson language [1], the parameters, J1.2/2J_{1.2}/2 and J1,2​ΔJ_{1,2}\Delta, correspond the hopping amplitudes and inter-site Coulomb repulsions, respectively.

A schematic phase diagram for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-KK X​X​ZXXZ model (1) is presented in Fig. 1. Here, the anisotropy is set to Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15 so as to locate the multi-critical (quantum triple) point

(J2,K)=(0.5,0),(J_{2},K)=(0.5,0), (2)

within the abscissa axis [3]. The X​YXY (superfluid), VBS, chiral VBS, and charge density wave (CDW) phases appear according to the preceeding studies, Ref. [3] and [1, 2]; in the former study [3], the case of the abscissa axis, K=0K=0, was clarified, whereas in the latter [1, 2], the ordinate axis J2=0J_{2}=0 (albeit, for Δ=0\Delta=0) was investigated in detail. Here, we follow the terminology of Ref. [1], because this paper deals with both K>0K>0 and K<0K<0 cases. The dashed (solid) line indicates that the phase transition is (dis)continuous [1, 2, 3]. The interaction parameters, J2J_{2} and KK, are swept along the line

Lδ:K=−6​(J2−0.5+δ),{\rm L}_{\delta}:\ K=-6(J_{2}-0.5+\delta), (3)

parameterized by δ\delta. As explained in Fig. 1, the parameter δ\delta indicates the distance from the multi-critical point (2), which plays a significant role in the crossover-scaling analysis. In order to analyze the X​YXY-VBS criticality reliably, the slope of the line Lδ is set to be parallel to the phase boundary between the VBS and chiral VBS phases. This technique is a key ingredient of the present finite-size-scaling analyses, where the extention of the parameter space J2J_{2}-KK is crucial. The crossover critical exponent ϕ\phi characterizes the power-law singularity of the phase boundary around the multi-critical point (2) [14, 15].

The ring-exchange term of the Hamiltonian (1) is rewritten as

2​K​∑[i​j​k​l](Six​Sjx​Skx​Slx+Siy​Sjy​Sky​Sly+Six​Sjx​Sky​Sly+Siy​Sjy​Skx​SlxCLOSE\displaystyle 2K\sum_{[ijkl]}(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{k}S^{x}_{l}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}S^{y}_{k}S^{y}_{l}+S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}S^{y}_{k}S^{y}_{l}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}S^{x}_{k}S^{x}_{l}
OPEN+Siy​Sjx​Skx​Sly+Six​Sjy​Sky​Slx−Six​Sjy​Skx​Sly−Siy​Sjx​Sky​Slx),\displaystyle+S^{y}_{i}S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{k}S^{y}_{l}+S^{x}_{i}S^{y}_{j}S^{y}_{k}S^{x}_{l}-S^{x}_{i}S^{y}_{j}S^{x}_{k}S^{y}_{l}-S^{y}_{i}S^{x}_{j}S^{y}_{k}S^{x}_{l}), (4)

in terms of the ordinary Six,yS_{i}^{x,y}-based representation [1]. It is a good position to introduce the JJ-QQ model [16, 17]. The plaquette interaction term of the “easy plane” [18] JJ-Q⟂Q_{\perp} model admits a neat expression

−Q⟂∑[i​j​k​l](Bi​jBk​l+Bi​lBj​k),-Q_{\perp}\sum_{[ijkl]}(B_{ij}B_{kl}+B_{il}B_{jk}), (5)

with the X​YXY interaction, Bi​j=2​(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)B_{ij}=2(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}). The plaquette interactions of the JJ-KK and JJ-Q⟂Q_{\perp} models differ significantly. In fact, the Q⟂Q_{\perp} interaction stabilizes the VBS phase, whereas the exceedingly large |K||K| stabilizes the CDW phase eventually, as shown in Fig. 1. It is claimed that the Q⟂Q_{\perp}-driven phase transition to the VBS phase would be discontinuous [18, 19].

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. 2, we present the numerical results. The high-order fidelity susceptibility as well as its scaling theory are explained. In Sec. 3, we address the summary and discussions.

2 Numerical results

In this section, we present the numerical results for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-KK X​X​ZXXZ model (1). We employed the exact diagonalization method for the rectangular cluster with N(=L2)≤62N(=L^{2})\leq 6^{2} spins. Here, the symbol LL denotes the linear dimension of the finite-size cluster. The total magnetization ∑iNSiz\sum_{i}^{N}S^{z}_{i} is fixed to

1and​ 1/2,1\ \ {\rm and}\ \ 1/2, (6)

(magnon’s dilution limit) for the even- and odd-NN clusters, respectively, so that these two series of data behave similarly; even- and odd-NN systems show distinctive behaviors, unless otherwise remedied. Moreover, it has been claimed that the VBS-Néel phase transition is detected sensitively by the inclusion of dilution [20].

In order to analyze the X​YXY-VBS phase transition, we utilize the high-order fidelity susceptibility [7, 8]

χF(3)=−∂λ3F(λ)|λ=0.\chi^{(3)}_{F}=-\partial_{\lambda}^{3}F(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}. (7)

Here, the fidelity FF is given by the overlap F⁡(λ)=|⟨λ|0⟩|F(\lambda)=|\langle\lambda|0\rangle| [21, 22, 23, 24] between the ground states |λ⟩|\lambda\rangle of proximate perturbation parameters, λ\lambda and (λ=)​0(\lambda=)0. The perturbed Hamiltonian ℋ+λ​V{\cal H}+\lambda V is given by

V=∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩𝒫i​jt0,V=\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}{\cal P}^{t_{0}}_{ij}, (8)

with the projection operator 𝒫i​jt0=|t0⟩i​j⟨t0|i​j{\cal P}^{t_{0}}_{ij}=|t_{0}\rangle_{ij}\ {}_{ij}\langle t_{0}| onto a triplet sector |t0⟩i​j=|+⟩i​|−⟩j+|−⟩i​|+⟩j2|t_{0}\rangle_{ij}=\frac{|+\rangle_{i}|-\rangle_{j}+|-\rangle_{i}|+\rangle_{j}}{\sqrt{2}} with zero longitudinal magnetic moment; here, the vector |±⟩i|\pm\rangle_{i} denotes the spin state at site ii. Note that the exact diagonalization method yields the ground-state vector |λ⟩|\lambda\rangle explicitly, and one is able to evaluate the fidelity F⁡(λ)=|⟨λ|0⟩|F(\lambda)=|\langle\lambda|0\rangle| straightforwardly. As would be apparent from the definition (8), the perturbation field VV is sensitive to the onset of the in-plane magnetization, namely, the X​YXY phase. The perturbation field VV is magnetic-moment-direction insensitive, and so, it is not a symmetry-breaking field. In a preliminary stage, we found that the singularities of the specific heat as well as the conventional fidelity susceptibility are hard to appreciate; possibly, the specific-heat critical exponent takes a negative value. Therefore, we resort to the high-order fidelity susceptibility χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F} to detect the criticality sensitively [7, 8].

According to the scaling theory [13, 25, 26], the high-order fidelity susceptibility obeys the scaling formula

χF(3)=Lx​f​((K−Kc)​L1/ν),\chi_{F}^{(3)}=L^{x}f\left((K-K_{c})L^{1/\nu}\right), (9)

with the critical point KcK_{c}, correlation-length critical exponent ν\nu, χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F}’s scaling dimension xx, and a scaling function ff; namely, the correlation length ξ\xi diverges as ξ∼|K−Kc|−ν\xi\sim|K-K_{c}|^{-\nu} at at the critical point. (Note that the parameters (J2,K)(J_{2},K) are swept along the line Lδ (3).) The scaling dimension xx is given by

x=3/ν,x=3/\nu, (10)

because the operator ∂λ\partial_{\lambda} in Eq. (7) has the scaling dimension 1/ν1/\nu, whereas the fidelity FF is dimensionless [13, 25, 26]. Hence, the high-order fidelity susceptibility has an enhanced scaling dimension. One is able to capture the signature for the criticality sensitively, even though the underlying singularity 1/ν1/\nu takes a small value.

2.1 X​YXY-VBS phase transition with Δ=0\Delta=0 and fixed δ\delta: High-order-fidelity-susceptibility χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} analysis

In this section, we analyze the X​YXY-VBS criticality via the probe χF(3)\chi^{(3)}_{F}. As for J2=0J_{2}=0 and Δ=0\Delta=0, the stochastic-series-expansion result [2] is available. The transition point was estimated as (J2​c,Kc)=(0,−3.95)(J_{2c},K_{c})=(0,-3.95) in our unit of energy, J1=1J_{1}=1. In order to detect this transition point, we set

δ=0.5+3.95/6.\delta=0.5+3.95/6. (11)

Then, the parameter-sweep line Lδ (3) passes the above-mentioned critical point (0,−3.95)(0,-3.95).

In Fig. 2, we present the high-order fidelity susceptibility χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} (7) for various KK, and (++) L=3L=3, (×\times) 44, (∗*) 55, and (□\Box) 66 with δ=0.5+3.95/6\delta=0.5+3.95/6 (11) and Δ=0\Delta=0. The peak of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} develops rapidly, as the system size LL enlarges. The peak indicates the onset of the X​YXY-VBS phase transition at K=KcK=K_{c}. For small K<KcK<K_{c}, the X​YXY phase is realized, whereas for large K>KcK>K_{c}, the VBS phase emerges. In contrast, the background, namely, contribution of the non-singular part, appears to be rather small. Such a feature is a merit of the high-order fidelity susceptibility, which picks up the singular part sensitively out of the background. Although the finite-size drift of the peak position seems to be non-negligible, the drift distance is governed by the scaling theory. According to the scaling formula (9), the drift distance δ​K\delta K should scale as ∼1/L1/ν\sim 1/L^{1/\nu}, and in a systematic manner, the critical point can be appreciated as follows.

In Fig. 3, we present the approximate critical point Kc∗​(L)K_{c}^{*}(L) for 1/L1/ν1/L^{1/\nu} with δ=0.5+3.95/6\delta=0.5+3.95/6 (11), Δ=0\Delta=0 and 1/ν=0.91/\nu=0.9. Here, the approximate critical point denotes the position of the χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} peak

∂χF(3)∂K|K=Kc∗​(L)=0,\frac{\partial\chi^{(3)}_{F}}{\partial K}|_{K=K_{c}^{*}(L)}=0, (12)

for each LL. As explained above, the abscissa scale 1/L1/ν1/L^{1/\nu} describes the finite-size drift of Kc∗​(L)K_{c}^{*}(L), and the validity of 1/ν=0.91/\nu=0.9 is considered afterward. The least-squares fit to the L=4L=4-66 data yields an estimate Kc=−3.76​(7)K_{c}=-3.76(7) in the thermodynamic limit L→∞L\to\infty. In order to appreciate a possible systematic error, replacing the abscissa scale 1/L1/ν1/L^{1/\nu} with a smaller exponent 1/ν=0.751/\nu=0.75, we made the similar analysis as that of Fig. 3. (This lower bound 1/ν=0.751/\nu=0.75 is considered afterward.) Thereby, we obtained an alternative value Kc=−4.18​(6)K_{c}=-4.18(6). The deviation ≈0.42\approx 0.42 from the above estimate appears to dominate the least-squares-fit error ≈0.07\approx 0.07, and it may indicate a possible systematic error. Therefore, considering the former as an indicator for the error margin we obtained

(J2​c,Kc)=[−0.032​(70),−3.76​(42)].(J_{2c},K_{c})=[-0.032(70),-3.76(42)]. (13)

The value of J2​cJ_{2c} comes from the propagation of uncertainty through the relation (3). The present result (13) agrees with the above-mentioned stochastic-series-expansion estimate (0,−3.95)(0,-3.95) [2], indicating that the available simulation data already enter into the scaling regime. Encouraged by this finding, we turn to the analysis of the inverse correlation-length critical exponent 1/ν1/\nu.

In Fig. 4, as the symbol (+)(+), we present the approximate inverse correlation-length critical exponent ν−1​(L)\nu^{-1}(L) for 1/L21/L^{2} with the same δ\delta and Δ\Delta as those of Fig. 2. Here, the approximate inverse correlation-length critical exponent is given by

ν−1​(L−1/2)=ln⁡χF(3)​(L)|K=Kc∗​(L)−ln⁡χF(3)​(L−1)|K=Kc∗​(L−1)3​(ln⁡L−ln⁡(L−1)),\nu^{-1}(L-1/2)=\frac{\ln\chi_{F}^{(3)}(L)|_{K=K_{c}^{*}(L)}-\ln\chi_{F}^{(3)}(L-1)|_{K=K_{c}^{*}(L-1)}}{3(\ln L-\ln(L-1))}, (14)

because χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}’s peak develops as ∼Lx\sim L^{x} with χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}’s scaling dimension x=3/νx=3/\nu (10). The least-squares fit to the (++) data yields an estimate 1/ν=0.91​(14)1/\nu=0.91(14) in the thermodynamic limit. Additionally, similar analyses were made for the values of (×\times) δ=1\delta=1, and (∗*) 1.41.4 with Δ=0\Delta=0, and the results are shown in Fig. 4. The least-squares fit to these data yields 1/ν=0.89​(27)1/\nu=0.89(27) and 0.957​(32)0.957(32), respectively. As shown in Fig. 4, around such an optimal regime of δ\delta, the ν−1​(L)\nu^{-1}(L) data indicate the value, 1/ν≈0.91/\nu\approx 0.9, and the deviation seems to be bounded by

1/ν=0.90​(15).1/\nu=0.90(15). (15)

The validity of this estimate is cross-checked in Sec. 2.2, where we make the scaling plot for χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} in order to examine its scaling behavior further in detail. As mentioned above, the ν−1​(L)\nu^{-1}(L) data exhibit a rather suppressed finite-size artifact. Such a feature was noticed by the pioneering fidelity-susceptibility analysis [12], where the two-dimensional cluster with only N≤20N\leq 20 spins yields reliable estimates for the critical exponents.

As a comparison, in Fig. 5, we show the ordinary second-order fidelity susceptibility χF(2)(=−∂λ2F|λ=0)\chi^{(2)}_{F}(=-\partial^{2}_{\lambda}F|_{\lambda=0}) (see Eq. (7)); here, the parameters are the same as those of Fig. 2. The scaling dimension of the ordinary fidelity susceptibility χF(2)\chi_{F}^{(2)} should be ≈1.8(=0.9⋅2)\approx 1.8(=0.9\cdot 2) (see Eq. (10) and (15)), which does not reach extensive-quantity’s dimensionality, 22. Therefore, it does not fit detailed analysis of criticality.

We address a number of remarks. First, the result 1/ν=0.90​(15)1/\nu=0.90(15) [Eq. (15)] appears to be substantially smaller than that of the 3D-X​YXY universality class, 1/ν(≈0.67−1)≈1.491/\nu(\approx 0.67^{-1})\approx 1.49 [27, 28], for instance. Therefore, it is suggested that the criticality belongs to a unique universality class. Last, the scaling dimension x=3/νx=3/\nu (10) of the high-order fidelity susceptibility is given solely by ν\nu, and we do not have to make any additional considerations of the order parameters and the associated scaling dimensions. We stress that the perturbation operator VV (8) is not a symmetry breaking field, and so, the scaling theory [13, 25, 26] applies to the present treatment. Hence, the present analyses are all closed within the ν\nu-mediated singularities.

2.2 X​YXY-VBS phase transition with Δ=0\Delta=0 and fixed δ\delta: Scaling plot of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}

In this section, as a crosscheck, we make the scaling plot for χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}, relying on the analysis in Sec. 2.1. For that purpose, we need to fix the scaling dimension xx of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}. Putting the exponent 1/ν=0.91/\nu=0.9 [Eq. (15)] into the scaling relation x=3/νx=3/\nu (10), we obtain χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}’s scaling dimension as

x=2.7.x=2.7. (16)

In Fig. 6, we present the scaling plot, (K−Kc)​L1/ν(K-K_{c})L^{1/\nu}-L−x​χF(3)L^{-x}\chi_{F}^{(3)}, for (++) L=4L=4, (×\times) 55, and (∗*) 66. Here, the parameters, δ=0.5+3.95/6\delta=0.5+3.95/6 (11) and Δ=0\Delta=0, are the same as those of Fig. 2. The scaling parameters are set to Kc=−3.76K_{c}=-3.76 [Eq. (13)], 1/ν=0.91/\nu=0.9 [Eq. (15)], and x=2.7x=2.7 [Eq. (16)]. The scaled data seem to collapse into a scaling curve satisfactorily. Particularly, the (×\times) L=5L=5 and (∗*) 66 data are about to overlap each other. Hence, the validity of the scaling analysis in Sec. 2.1 is confirmed; the corrections to finite-size scaling seems to be rather small, as observed in Sec. 2.1. We stress that there is no ad hoc adjustable parameter undertaken in the scaling plot, Fig. 6.

This is a good position to address an overview on the related studies of the critical exponent ν\nu. To the best of author’s knowledge, little attention has been paid to the X​YXY-VBS critical exponents for the X​YXY (U(1)(1) symmetric) frustrated magnet. On the one hand, as for the Heisenberg (SU(2)(2) symmetric) magnet, the frustration-driven phase transition from the Néel phase to the quantum disordered state has been studied rather extensively [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. As shown in Table 1, various frustrated magnets such as the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-QQ [29], J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} [30, 31, 32], and J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} [33] Heisenberg models, have been simulated with the exact diagonalization (ED), tensor product states (TPSs), restricted Boltzmann machine combined with pair product states (RBM++PP), projected entangled pair state (PEPS), and tensor network (TN) methods, respectively. The estimated correlation-length critical exponents seem to be unsettled. Almost all values are larger than that of the ordinary 3D-X​YXY universality class ν≈0.67\nu\approx 0.67 [27, 28], indicating that a novel class of phase transition may set in. The present estimate ν=1.11​(19)\nu=1.11(19) for the U(1)(1)-symmetric case also exhibits a tendency for an enhancement, as compared to that of the 3D-X​YXY universality class.

Last, we address a remark on the conventional (second order) fidelity susceptibility χF(2)\chi_{F}^{(2)}. Because the correlation-length critical exponent takes a large value, ν(=0.9−1)≈1.11\nu(=0.9^{-1})\approx 1.11, the scaling dimension of the conventional fidelity susceptibility, x(2)(=2/ν)≈1.8x^{(2)}(=2/\nu)\approx 1.8 [13, 25, 26], does not reach extensive-quantity’s scaling L2L^{2} in two spatial dimensions. Therefore, the conventional fidelity susceptibility does not capture the underlying singularity properly.

2.3 Multi-criticality of the X​YXY-VBS phase boundary: Crossover-scaling analysis of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}

In this section, we investigate the end-point singularity of the X​YXY-VBS phase boundary at the multi-critical point J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5. For that purpose, we turn on the anisotropy parameter Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15 in this section; see Introduction. We then resort to the crossover-scaling theory [14, 15], where the distance from the multi-critical point δ\delta is incorporated into the scaling formula (9) accompanying the crossover critical exponent ϕ\phi. The crossover-scaling formula is given by the expression

χF(3)=Lx˙​g​((K−Kc​(δ))​L1/ν˙,δ​Lϕ/ν˙),\chi^{(3)}_{F}=L^{\dot{x}}g\left((K-K_{c}(\delta))L^{1/\dot{\nu}},\delta L^{\phi/\dot{\nu}}\right), (17)

with the phase-transition point Kc​(δ)K_{c}(\delta) for δ\delta, and a scaling function gg. Here, the multi-critical exponents, x˙\dot{x} and ν˙\dot{\nu}, denote χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}’s scaling dimension and correlation-length critical exponent, respectively, right at δ=0\delta=0. The crossover critical exponent ϕ\phi describes the singular part of the phase boundary [14, 15]

Kc​(δ)∼−δ1/ϕ,K_{c}(\delta)\sim-\delta^{1/\phi}, (18)

toward δ→0+\delta\to 0^{+} (J2→0.5−J_{2}\to 0.5^{-}).

Before commencing the crossover-scaling analysis of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}, we fix the multi-critical exponents, ϕ\phi, ν˙\dot{\nu}, and x˙\dot{x}. We make a proposition that the phase boundary (see Eq. (18)) terminates linearly at δ=0\delta=0 (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5)

ϕ=1.\phi=1. (19)

Such a linearity implies that the phase boundary Kc​(δ)∼−δK_{c}(\delta)\sim-\delta could be interpreted as a self-dual line [34, 35]. In Ref. [34], the duality between the VBS and easy-plane-Néel phases is argued for the easy-plane-JJ-QQ and bose-Hubbard models. As for the multi-critical correlation-length critical exponent, we accept

ν˙=0.5.\dot{\nu}=0.5. (20)

This exponent was obtained by the above-mentioned duality analysis of the simulation results [34], as well as the hyperscaling relation α˙=2−(d+z)​ν˙\dot{\alpha}=2-(d+z)\dot{\nu} with the spacial dimensionality d=2d=2, multi-critical specific-heat critical exponent α˙=0\dot{\alpha}=0 (mean-field), and the dynamical critical exponent z=2z=2 [36, 37, 38, 39]. The hyperscaling relation holds generically [26], and it was derived for the fully-frustrated magnets (Lifshitz criticality) field-theoretically [36, 37, 38, 39]; the above value z=2z=2 is taken from this argument in the mean-field limit. The value z=2z=2 indicates that the imaginary-time correlation length ξτ\xi_{\tau} diverges as ξτ∼ξ2\xi_{\tau}\sim\xi^{2} (ξ\xi: real-space correlation length). The imaginary-time correlation length is substantially longer than the real-space one. In the exact-diagonalization analysis, one does not have to care about this space-time anisotropy, because at the ground state, the inverse temperature β\beta diverges as β→∞\beta\to\infty, which covers ξτ(≪β)\xi_{\tau}(\ll\beta). Therefore, in the following crossover-scaling analysis, we are allowed to concentrate only on the real-space sector, LL. Lastly, putting ν˙=0.5\dot{\nu}=0.5 [Eq. (20)] into the scaling relation (10), we obtain the multi-critical scaling dimension of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}

x˙=6.\dot{x}=6. (21)

In Fig. 7, we present the crossover scaling plot, (K−Kc​(δ))​L1/ν˙(K-K_{c}(\delta))L^{1/\dot{\nu}}-L−x˙​χF(3)L^{-\dot{x}}\chi_{F}^{(3)}, for various system sizes (++) L=4L=4, (×\times) 55, and (∗*) 66, with the anisotropy parameter Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15 and the multi-critical scaling dimension x˙=6\dot{x}=6 (21). The second argument of the crossover-scaling formula (17) is fixed to δ​Lϕ/ν˙=25\delta L^{\phi/\dot{\nu}}=25 with ϕ=1\phi=1 (19) and ν˙=0.5\dot{\nu}=0.5 (20), and the critical point KcK_{c} is determined via the same scheme as that of Sec. 2.1. The crossover-scaled data appear to collapse into a scaling curve satisfactorily. Particularly, the (×\times) L=5L=5 and (∗*) 66 data are about to overlap each other.

We address a number of remarks. First, the crossover critical exponent ϕ=1\phi=1 is supported. As mentioned above, this result indicates that the phase boundary is interpreted as a self-dual line. In the above-mentioned X​YXY-paramagnetic phase boundary [36, 38, 39] for the frustrated magnet, the crossover critical exponent takes ϕ<1\phi<1, and the phase boundary should curve convexly as in Eq. (18); in this case, the X​YXY and paramagnetic phases are not dual, as anticipated. Last, the exponent 1/ν=0.91/\nu=0.9 (15) in the scaling plot, Fig. 6, and the multi-critical exponent 1/ν˙=21/\dot{\nu}=2 (20) in the crossover-scaling plot, Fig. 7, differ significantly. Hence, the underlying singularities behind these scaling plots are not identical, and the overlap of the crossover-scaling plot is by no means accidental.

3 Summary and discussions

The J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-KK X​X​ZXXZ model (1) was investigated with the exact diagonalization method. The X​YXY-VBS phase transition was analyzed with the high-order fidelity susceptibility χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} (7) [7, 8], which is readily evaluated via the exact diagonalization scheme. As a preliminary survey, with Δ=0\Delta=0 and δ=0.5+3.95/6\delta=0.5+3.95/6 (11) fixed, we evaluated χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)}, and obtained the critical point (J2​c,Kc)=(−0.032​(70),−3.76​(42))(J_{2c},K_{c})=(-0.032(70),-3.76(42)) (13). The estimate agrees with the stochastic-series-expansion result (J2​c,Kc)=(0,−3.95)(J_{2c},K_{c})=(0,-3.95) [2]. Thereby, we analyzed the inverse correlation-length critical exponent 1/ν1/\nu via the scaling behavior of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} with Δ=0\Delta=0 and fixed δ\delta. We estimate the exponent as 1/ν=0.9​(15)1/\nu=0.9(15) [Eq. (15)], and made a comparison with those obtained for the frustrated Heisenberg magnets [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. We then turn to the analysis of the crossover-criticality toward δ→0+\delta\to 0^{+} (J2→0.5−J_{2}\to 0.5^{-}) under the setting Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15. With crossover-scaling the δ\delta parameter properly, the χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} data were cast into the crossover-scaling formula (17) under the propositions, ϕ=1\phi=1 (19) and ν˙=0.5\dot{\nu}=0.5 (20). Thereby, we found that the crossover-scaled data fall into a scaling curve satisfactorily. The linearity of the phase boundary ϕ=1\phi=1 implies that the phase boundary is interpreted as a self-dual line, as claimed for the easy-plane JJ-QQ magnet [34, 35].

The scaling dimension x=3/νx=3/\nu (10) of χF(3)\chi_{F}^{(3)} is given solely by ν\nu, and the undertaken analyses are closed within the ν\nu-mediated singularities. Rather intriguingly, according to the duality theory [34], the ν\nu value is related to the anomalous dimensions of the order parameters beside the phase boundary. It is tempting to consider those order parameters and the associated anomalous dimensions. This problem is left for the future study.
